rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The decision-making capacity given to Lot arises from purity of intellect and nature; knowledge here means knowledge of prophethood.
rows.anchor: “power of decision making” mentioned in the verse is concerned, it is the consequence of purity in intellect and nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's chosen prophets were the finest people, refining their innate abilities until worthy of revelation; revelation then supplemented their inner light with divine light.
rows.anchor: They developed their innate abilities until their inner self was fully refined and became worthy of receiving divine revelation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot was delivered from the city of evil and migrated to Syria with Abraham.
rows.anchor: he too migrated to Syria along with Abraham (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Delivered” means Lot was made safe from the punishment that struck his people.
rows.anchor: The word “delivered” has been used to show that he was rendered safe from the punishment that visited his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “abominable acts” primarily refer to homosexuality.
rows.anchor: The expression “abominable acts” primarily refers to their homosexuality.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural “acts” signals that such an evil habit brings many other evils with it wherever it takes hold in a nation.
rows.anchor: the plural shows that such an evil habit is never alone: wherever it surfaces in a nation, it brings with it a host of other evils too.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other evils are left unnamed because their heinousness makes them unworthy even of mention.
rows.anchor: they are not named because such is their heinous nature that they are not even worthy of mention.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their wickedness explains both Lot's rescue and their punishment: God did not want His righteous servants to remain among the wicked.
rows.anchor: God did not want His pious and righteous people to stay among the wicked and wretched ones.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mercy granted to Lot means worldly security and success in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The word “mercy” refers to the success they achieved in this world by being rendered secure and also the success they will achieve in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah is accusative because the preceding verses imply an omitted clause comparing God's help to earlier prophets with His help to Noah.
rows.anchor: is due to the meaning that emanates from the previous verses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied sense is that, just as God helped the preceding prophets, He likewise delivered Noah and came to his aid.
rows.anchor: Just as We showed mercy to the afore-mentioned prophets, delivered and helped them, in a similar way, We delivered Noah too and came to His help.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse points to Noah's final supplication in Sūrah Nūḥ; its closing verses give the prayer, while its acceptance is explained there.
rows.anchor: The verse refers to the final supplication of Noah (sws) that is mentioned in S ūrah Nūḥ and which makes the heart tremble.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ahl refers not only to a person's family but also to his companions and followers; Islahi says he discussed this under Ṭāhā 132.
rows.anchor: It refers not only to a person’s family but also to his companions and followers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “grave calamity” includes the persecution Noah and his followers endured from truth's enemies and the final torment that destroyed them.
rows.anchor: The expression “a grave calamity” refers to the affliction Noah (sws) and his followers suffered at the hands of the enemies of the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition min after “We rescued” signals an understood verb meaning “We took revenge,” yielding a translation that says God helped Noah and avenged revelation-deniers.
rows.anchor: We helped him and took revenge from the people who denied Our revelations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse briefly alludes to the deniers' crimes; their details appear in earlier sūrahs and later in Sūrah Nūḥ.
rows.anchor: The verse very concisely refers to their crimes. Details can be seen in the earlier sūrahs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah's period of warning had no parallel in duration.
rows.anchor: the extent of time period in which Noah (sws) tried to warn his nation bears no parallel.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah Nūḥ depicts Noah's compassionate, devoted efforts to awaken his people from heedlessness.
rows.anchor: In Sūrah Nūḥ, the way he compassionately and devotedly went upon trying to awaken his nation from their slumber can be seen.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people were so hard-hearted that Noah's appeals did not move them, and God ultimately drowned the whole nation.
rows.anchor: so hard-hearted were these people that nothing could impact them. Ultimately, they were punished for this and the whole nation was drowned by the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their drowning is pictured as cleansing the earth of a pile of filth, with water from heaven and earth sent at God's command.
rows.anchor: It was as if the whole nation was a pile of filth that was cleansed from the face of the earth by water from heavens and the earth at God’s behest.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the flood, God again settled Noah and his followers on earth.
rows.anchor: After that, God once again made Noah (sws) and his followers inhabit the earth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah's account would aid full understanding, but Sūrah Nūḥ is the more appropriate place to study the story.
rows.anchor: it would have been better if its description in the Torah could be studied. However, a more appropriate place for this study is Sūrah Nūḥ.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding prophets were presented chronologically as founders of their peoples; the next passage turns to prophets whose conduct offers exemplary character for all.
rows.anchor: In the preceding verses, those prophets were mentioned in the chronological order who were founders of their nations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David and Solomon introduce the exemplary figures as humble kings, granted grandeur yet remaining grateful to God.
rows.anchor: Both were best examples of kings with a very humble temperament. They were blessed by God with majesty and splendour but they remained thankful to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David and Solomon were not led astray by royal grandeur; they used their resources and abilities to please God.
rows.anchor: and were never misled by their grandeur.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Job, Ishmael, Idrīs, and Dhū al-Kifl exemplify patience and perseverance through severe trials.
rows.anchor: They outshone human beings with regard to their patience and perseverance. God put them through severe trials but they remained steadfast in each.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage names Jonah, Zacharias, and Mary in connection with desperate appeals to God, which He answered through special mercy, making the impossible possible.
rows.anchor: After that Jonah (sws), Zacharias (sws) and Mary (sws) are mentioned. They called upon their Lord in hopeless and desperate circumstances.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These messengers' lives teach the sūra's addressees not to become arrogant when granted divine favors and blessings.
rows.anchor: There is a great lesson in the lives of these messengers for the addressees of this sūrah who were showing arrogance on being granted favours and blessings from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These examples also guide the Prophet's oppressed Companions, who were facing precarious trials and could see only darkness ahead.
rows.anchor: they also provide guidance to the oppressed companions of the Prophet (sws) who at that time were passing through very precarious trials and could see nothing but darkness in front of them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David and Solomon appear in the accusative because the context supplies an omitted verb, as with Noah earlier; the translation makes that verb explicit.
rows.anchor: The nouns David and Solomon occur in the text in their accusative form just as is the case with Noah earlier on is.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term refers to cattle and goats grazing at night.
rows.anchor: refers to the grazing of cattle and goats at night.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine pronoun in fafahhamnāhā refers to an antecedent supplied by context; Islahi notes similar examples in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: occurs in deference to the antecedent that is evident from the context.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute concerned goats entering another person's cultivated field at night; David ruled, but young Solomon offered a sounder and fairer judgment, which David adopted.
rows.anchor: a herd of goats belonging to someone had barged into the cultivated fields of another person. David (sws) pronounced his verdict in this matter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic purpose is not to disclose the verdicts' details but to show David's care: once his young son's reasoning revealed an error, he promptly changed his ruling and accepted advice from a junior, inexperienced person.
rows.anchor: as soon as he realized his mistake on the basis of his young son’s opinion, he immediately changed his decision and accepted the opinion of someone junior and inexperienced.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode also highlights Solomon's remarkable youthful judgment and the respect his illustrious father gave his advice, including in governance.
rows.anchor: he would at times advise his illustrious father

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi regards exegetes' added details about the dispute as extraneous and conjectural, so he declines to speculate about possible scenarios.
rows.anchor: Our exegetes have presented the details of a dispute that is totally extraneous to the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's observation of the matter means He continued overseeing this family's rule after giving them political leadership and assessed their sensitivity to His guidance.
rows.anchor: after granting the reins of political leadership to this family, God did not become aloof of its affairs. He continued to observe their governance
